source.version: Journal version of record: Computers in Human Behavior: Artificial Humans 4 (2025) 100140; received 30 December 2024, revised 12 March 2025, accepted 19 March 2025, available online 19 March 2025 (p. 1)
source.title_on_document: If ChatGPT can do it, where is my creativity? generative AI boosts performance but diminishes experience in creative writing

supplement.where: Appendix A: 'Supplementary data to this article can be found online at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chbah.2025.100140' (p. 13)
supplement.holds: SI Table 1 (demographics by group), SI Table 2 (ICC scores among the four raters), SI Table 3 (regressions of performance on treatment, by group and pooled across groups), SI Table 4 (HAI dyad analysis), SI Table 5 (group-level creativity), SI Table 6 (perception regressions). The main text gives performance results mostly as Fig. 2 means with 95 percent CIs plus a few b/SE/p values; arm sizes and the pooled treatment coefficients are only in the SI.

paper_design_summary: 225 UK university students recruited on Prolific (266 completed, 43 dropped for failing an attention check) were quota-sampled into four groups by native English and prior ChatGPT use, then randomly assigned between subjects to use ChatGPT (AI condition) or not use it (control) for a 10-minute task: a short piece (about 100 words) describing as many uses as possible for a hypothetical 'printer that can print anything in 2097'. Output was scored for fluency (frequency: number of uses) and flexibility (number of distinct conceptual domains) by GPT-4o/GPT-4 Turbo with human validation, and for grammar errors and clarity suggestions with Grammarly; pre/post self-reported perceptions (value, enjoyment, difficulty, effort, trust, moral acceptance) were also collected.

studies.label: Online experiment: ChatGPT vs no ChatGPT on a 'printer in 2097' uses-writing task

assignment.what_was_assigned: Use of ChatGPT for the writing task (AI condition, explicitly asked to use ChatGPT) vs control (forbidden from using ChatGPT); assignment within four quota groups defined by English proficiency and prior ChatGPT experience
assignment.quote: After the pre-task survey, the experiment used a between-subjects design to randomly assign participants into one of two treatment conditions: the control condition (these participants were forbidden from using ChatGPT for the task)
assignment.locator: p. 5, Section 2.2 Design; also p. 4, Fig. 1 caption

arms.name: AI condition
arms.description: Participants 'were explicitly asked to make sure they used ChatGPT for the task'; self-reported usage: 27 % relied entirely on ChatGPT, 47 % made minor or major changes to AI output, 21 % used own prompts or a feedback loop, 5 % unclassified (p. 6)

arms.name: Control condition
arms.description: Participants were forbidden from using ChatGPT for the task; 90 % self-reported using no digital tools (p. 6)

participants.exclusions: 266 participants completed the study; 43 who failed the attention check were excluded, leaving 225. The paper does not say whether the attention check came before or after assignment, and does not give arm sizes in the main text (subgroup sizes 58, 60, 54, 53 are given for the four quota groups pooled across arms).
participants.who: Current students at UK universities recruited via Prolific (60 % undergraduates, 31 % postgraduates); mean age 29.07; four quota groups: non-native inexperienced n = 58, native inexperienced n = 60, non-native experienced n = 54, native experienced n = 53
participants.quote: A total of 266 participants completed the study, all current students studying at a university in the United Kingdom. [...] Forty-three people who failed the attention check were excluded from further analysis, leaving a final sample of 225.
participants.locator: p. 4, Section 2.1 Participants; p. 4, Section 2.2 (group ns)

ai_tool.how_used: Free use of ChatGPT to produce the written piece; participants reported tool usage after the task. Usage ranged from fully AI-written text to edited AI text to iterative prompting (p. 6, Section 3.2.2).

task.description: Alternate-uses style writing task: write a short piece (approx. 100 words) describing uses for a hypothetical 'printer that can print anything in 2097', instructed to 'describe as many unique uses as possible for this printer, AND do so as quickly as possible in 10 minutes' while minimising grammar errors and maximising clarity. The paper calls it a creative writing task.

outcomes.name: Frequency (fluency): number of different uses
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Count of distinct uses per submission identified by an LLM (GPT-4o and GPT-4 Turbo, temperature 0, few-shot prompt). Validated on a random sample of 40 responses annotated by three blinded human raters from the research team: human ICC 0.81; human vs GPT-4o ICC 0.93 for frequency (p. 5, Section 2.3; SI Table 2).

contrasts.reported: Fig. 2: AI-arm mean frequency above control in Groups 1, 3 and 4 (means with 95 % CIs, no numbers printed); Group 2 (Native, Inexperienced): b = 0.91, SE = 2.30, p = .69; Group 4: 'No significant differences were found in flexibility, correctness, frequency, or clarity'. Pooled and per-group regressions in SI Table 3 (not in this PDF).

outcomes.name: Flexibility: number of unique conceptual domains among a participant's uses
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Count of unique conceptual domains per submission identified by GPT-4o/GPT-4 Turbo with few-shot prompt; human ICC 0.81, human vs GPT-4o ICC 0.83 for flexibility (p. 5, Section 2.3).

contrasts.reported: Fig. 2: AI-arm mean flexibility above control in all four groups (means with 95 % CIs, no numbers printed); text: in Group 4 'No significant differences were found in flexibility'. Regressions in SI Table 3 (not in this PDF).

outcomes.name: Inaccuracy: number of grammar mistakes (Grammarly)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Writing-quality measure, not creativity: count of grammar mistakes (spelling, grammar, punctuation) detected by Grammarly; lower is better (p. 5, Section 2.3).

contrasts.reported: Fig. 2: AI arm has fewer grammar errors than control in all four groups (means with 95 % CIs, no numbers printed); Group 4 no significant difference. SI Table 3.

outcomes.name: Unclarity: number of clarity suggestions (Grammarly)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Writing-quality measure, not creativity: number of Grammarly suggestions for word choice, sentence structure, tone adjustments; lower is better (p. 5, Section 2.3).

contrasts.reported: Fig. 2 means with 95 % CIs; Group 2 (Native, Inexperienced): b = -1.30, SE = 1.90, p = .51; Group 3 (Non-Native, Experienced): b = -2.30, SE = 1.50, p = .14; Group 4 not significant; Group 1 lower in AI arm per Fig. 2. SI Table 3.

outcomes.name: Group-level frequency: number of different uses pooled across all participants in a condition
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Count of different uses across the pooled outputs of all participants in a condition (and in subgroups of it); the pooled total (552 control) is below the sum of subgroup totals, which suggests de-duplication across participants, but the paper does not define the computation. Counts are not normalised for arm size, and arm sizes are not in the main text. The paper frames these group-level results as evidence on 'diversity of ideas' (p. 10, Section 4.2.3).

contrasts.reported: Fig. 5 bottom panel (Frequency), control vs AI: Grp 9 all participants 552 vs 635; Grp 1 193 vs 140; Grp 2 189 vs 198; Grp 3 136 vs 189; Grp 4 161 vs 221; Grp 5 non-native 302 vs 315; Grp 6 native 312 vs 397; Grp 7 inexperienced 344 vs 312; Grp 8 experienced 283 vs 370. Text p. 7 reverses the Grp 9 labels: 'Flexibility (635 vs. 552) and Frequency (442 vs. 313)'. No test statistic; SI Table 5.

diversity_detail.metric: Number of different uses in the pooled outputs of a condition
diversity_detail.computed_over: All outputs of a condition (or subgroup) pooled into one set
diversity_detail.uncertainty: None reported in the main text (single counts per set)
diversity_detail.notes: Not adjusted for unequal arm sizes; computation of de-duplication not described.

outcomes.name: Group-level flexibility: number of unique uses/domains pooled across all participants in a condition
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Fig. 5 caption labels flexibility as 'numbers of unique uses' at group level; pooled total (313 control) is below the sum of subgroup totals, suggesting de-duplication across participants. Not normalised for arm size. Fig. 5 caption also swaps the colour labels ('red colour indicating using ChatGPT (the Control condition) and blue for not using ChatGPT (the AI condition)'); the legend shows Control red, AI blue.

contrasts.reported: Fig. 5 top panel (Flexibility), control vs AI: Grp 9 all participants 313 vs 442; Grp 1 74 vs 88; Grp 2 62 vs 138; Grp 3 101 vs 126; Grp 4 127 vs 175; Grp 5 non-native 156 vs 192; Grp 6 native 179 vs 293; Grp 7 inexperienced 122 vs 196; Grp 8 experienced 212 vs 275. No test statistic; SI Table 5.

diversity_detail.metric: Number of unique uses/conceptual domains in the pooled outputs of a condition
diversity_detail.computed_over: All outputs of a condition (or subgroup) pooled into one set
diversity_detail.uncertainty: None reported in the main text (single counts per set)
diversity_detail.notes: Not adjusted for unequal arm sizes; text on p. 7 swaps the Grp 9 flexibility and frequency numbers relative to Fig. 5.

eligibility.reason: Students were randomly assigned between subjects to use ChatGPT or not (p. 5, Section 2.2); 225 people analyzed (p. 4); fluency and flexibility were counted on the written output by an LLM validated against human raters (p. 5). Arm sizes are not in the main text, and control compliance is self-reported (10 % of controls reported some digital-tool use).

one_line_finding: Among 225 UK students, those randomly assigned to use ChatGPT listed more uses (frequency) and more distinct domains (flexibility) with fewer grammar errors and in less time than controls in most of four subgroups, shown as means with 95 % CIs in Fig. 2 (p. 6); numeric regression results are in SI Table 3.
open_questions: Arm sizes (AI vs control) and the pooled treatment coefficients for frequency and flexibility are only in the SI (Table 3), which is not in this PDF.
Whether the 43 attention-check exclusions happened before or after random assignment is not stated.

How group-level counts in Fig. 5 were computed (de-duplication across participants) and whether they are comparable given unequal arm sizes; text on p. 7 swaps the Grp 9 flexibility and frequency numbers relative to Fig. 5.
Whether 'frequency' measured by an LLM should be coded measure category_count or automated_score.
notes: Outcomes not listed because they are not scored on the output: writing time (time spent completing the task; AI arm faster), and pre-to-post changes in self-reported value, enjoyment, intellectual difficulty, effort, trust and moral acceptance of AI (Fig. 6, p. 10; Section 3.3; SI Table 6). Also not listed: the HAI dyad comparison (Human-only, AI-only, AI-led, Dyadic; Fig. 4, p. 8; SI Table 4), which groups participants by self-reported usage and is not randomized, and the demographic heterogeneity analysis (Fig. 3, p. 7). Task is coded divergent_test because it asks for as many uses as possible of a hypothetical object and is scored on fluency and flexibility; the paper calls it a creative writing task. Participants were quota-selected into four strata (English proficiency x prior ChatGPT experience) and then randomized within the design; the paper says this 'ensured balanced representation across both control and experimental conditions' (p. 4).
